proof_nl: Interpret the sign convention in T_t as follows: +1 means apply U and -1 means apply D. For a vector v=(v_1,...,v_L), write rev(v)=(v_L,...,v_1), and write c dot y for the usual dot product. For the induction only, let Alt_0^+=Alt_0^- be the empty sign string. I prove the following stronger statement by induction on k>=0: for every length L>=1 there exists a positive nondecreasing vector c_{L,k} of length L such that for every nonnegative vector y of length L, (i) if y is nondecreasing, then Total(T_t(y)) <= c_{L,k} dot y for every sign string t of length k, while Total(T_{Alt_k^-}(y)) = c_{L,k} dot y; if y is nonconstant, equality holds only for t=Alt_k^-; (ii) if y is nonincreasing, then Total(T_t(y)) <= rev(c_{L,k}) dot y for every sign string t of length k, while Total(T_{Alt_k^+}(y)) = rev(c_{L,k}) dot y; if y is nonconstant, equality holds only for t=Alt_k^+. The lemma is the case L=m and k=r. Base case k=0: the only sign string is the empty string, and c_{L,0}=(1,...,1) works because Total(T_empty(y))=Total(y)=c_{L,0} dot y. Now assume the statement holds for k and all lengths. Fix L, and let c=c_{L+1,k}. Define b=c_{L,k+1} by b_i = sum_{j=L+2-i}^{L+1} c_j for 1<=i<=L. Since c is positive, b_{i+1}-b_i = c_{L+1-i} > 0, so b is positive and strictly increasing, hence nondecreasing. Also, for every y=(y_1,...,y_L), expanding the definitions gives c dot U(y) = sum_{j=1}^{L+1} c_j sum_{i=1}^{j-1} y_i = sum_{i=1}^L (sum_{j=i+1}^{L+1} c_j) y_i = rev(b) dot y, and rev(c) dot D(y) = sum_{j=1}^{L+1} c_{L+2-j} sum_{i=j}^L y_i = sum_{i=1}^L (sum_{j=1}^i c_{L+2-j}) y_i = b dot y. Now let y be nonnegative and nondecreasing, and let t=(eps,u) with eps in {+1,-1} and u of length k. Since U(y)_{j+1}-U(y)_j = y_j >= 0, U(y) is nonnegative and nondecreasing; hence if eps=+1, the induction hypothesis gives Total(T_t(y)) = Total(T_u(U(y))) <= c dot U(y) = rev(b) dot y. Since D(y)_j-D(y)_{j+1} = y_j >= 0, D(y) is nonnegative and nonincreasing; hence if eps=-1, the induction hypothesis gives Total(T_t(y)) = Total(T_u(D(y))) <= rev(c) dot D(y) = b dot y. Because b is strictly increasing and y is nondecreasing, b dot y - rev(b) dot y = sum_{i=1}^{floor(L/2)} (b_{L+1-i}-b_i)(y_{L+1-i}-y_i) >= 0. If y is nonconstant, then y_L>y_1, so the i=1 term is positive; hence b dot y > rev(b) dot y. Therefore Total(T_t(y)) <= b dot y for every t. Also Alt_{k+1}^- = (-1,Alt_k^+), so Total(T_{Alt_{k+1}^-}(y)) = Total(T_{Alt_k^+}(D(y))) = rev(c) dot D(y) = b dot y, by the induction hypothesis. Thus b dot y is the maximum. If y is nonconstant and equality holds for some t, then the strict inequality b dot y > rev(b) dot y forces eps=-1. Since y is nonnegative and nonconstant, Total(y)>0, so D(y)_1=Total(y)>0=D(y)_{L+1}; hence D(y) is nonconstant. The induction hypothesis applied to D(y) then forces u=Alt_k^+, so t=Alt_{k+1}^-. This proves part (i) for k+1. For part (ii), let y be nonnegative and nonincreasing. If eps=+1, then U(y) is nonnegative and nondecreasing, so Total(T_t(y)) <= c dot U(y) = rev(b) dot y. If eps=-1, then D(y) is nonnegative and nonincreasing, so Total(T_t(y)) <= rev(c) dot D(y) = b dot y. Since y is nonincreasing, rev(b) dot y - b dot y = sum_{i=1}^{floor(L/2)} (b_{L+1-i}-b_i)(y_i-y_{L+1-i}) >= 0, and if y is nonconstant then y_1>y_L, so again the i=1 term is positive; hence rev(b) dot y > b dot y. Therefore Total(T_t(y)) <= rev(b) dot y for every t. Also Alt_{k+1}^+ = (+1,Alt_k^-), so Total(T_{Alt_{k+1}^+}(y)) = Total(T_{Alt_k^-}(U(y))) = c dot U(y) = rev(b) dot y. If y is nonconstant and equality holds, then eps=+1. Also U(y)_1=0 < Total(y)=U(y)_{L+1}, so U(y) is nonconstant; hence the induction hypothesis forces u=Alt_k^-, so t=Alt_{k+1}^+. This proves part (ii). The induction is complete. Taking L=m and k=r gives exactly the statement: if x is nonincreasing, then Total(T_t(x)) <= Total(T_{Alt_r^+}(x)) for every sign string t of length r, with equality iff t=Alt_r^+ when x is nonconstant; and if x is nondecreasing, then Total(T_t(x)) <= Total(T_{Alt_r^-}(x)) for every t, with equality iff t=Alt_r^- when x is nonconstant.
solver_summary: I proved a stronger induction statement with coefficient vectors. For each length L and number of steps k there is a positive increasing vector c_{L,k} such that on nondecreasing inputs the maximum value is c_{L,k} dot y and is attained by Alt_k^-, while on nonincreasing inputs the maximum is rev(c_{L,k}) dot y and is attained by Alt_k^+; the induction step uses the identities c dot U(y)=rev(b) dot y and rev(c) dot D(y)=b dot y for a strictly increasing b, and then compares b dot y with rev(b) dot y by pairing symmetric indices.
vetter_reason: The proof gives a complete induction on the number of steps, with a stronger weighted-linear-functional statement that cleanly handles both monotonicity cases and uniqueness. The key algebraic identities for U and D are derived correctly, the comparison between b·y and rev(b)·y is justified explicitly, and the equality cases are handled by strictness plus the induction hypothesis. No forbidden or undeclared dependencies are used. The only minor issue is that the proof fixes the convention +1->U and -1->D because the natural-language statement is slightly ambiguous there, but this is not a mathematical gap.
